title: Where it's followed
hookLine: Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia

lines: A TIMETABLE THAT IS A MAP.
cards: On the wall of some mosques, and in some prayer apps, the afternoon prayer has two start times. Asr, standard. Asr, Hanafi.
The Hanafi one comes later. Same sun, same city, same day. The difference is a shadow.
In the Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali books, Asr begins when an object's shadow grows as long as the object. The Hanafi school, following Abu Hanifa's view, waits until it's twice as long.
So a timetable for a city with both prints both lines, and each person knows which is theirs. That second line is a small map. It tells you the school traveled.

teach.b: Back on day 110 you met the word madhhab: a way, a path someone takes. The Hanafi way left Kufa early.
Abu Yusuf sat as a judge for the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, and judges trained in the school's books went out with the courts.
The Ottomans made it the law of their courts, from Istanbul across Anatolia and the Balkans, so a Muslim in Sarajevo, Skopje or Istanbul is often praying the way the Hanafi books describe.
In Central Asia, in cities like Bukhara and Samarkand, Hanafi scholars wrote major works of the school.
In South Asia, the Mughal court commissioned a large collection of Hanafi rulings, the Fatawa 'Alamgiri, one reason the school is followed in Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Afghanistan.
Some writers call it the most followed school, pointing to the size of the regions it covers.
There's no precise count, and some Muslims simply pray the way their parents and local mosque do, without naming a madhhab at all.
And a map doesn't show this: in each of those places, Hanafis live beside Shafi'is, Malikis, Hanbalis and Ja'fari Shia, sometimes in the same mosque. Hence two lines for Asr on one wall.

teach.h: THE WAYS CROSS IN ONE MOSQUE.
teach.b: Each school is a way someone goes, and the ways cross.

how: Hanafi Muslims across Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia follow the school's rulings on prayer, fasting and family law, and prayer timetables in mixed cities may list a separate Hanafi time for the afternoon prayer.

games.q: your prayer app shows two times for the afternoon prayer, a standard one and a later Hanafi one. why?
o: the schools measure the start by different shadow lengths.
games.why: same prayer, same sun. the other Sunni schools start Asr when a shadow equals the object; the Hanafi school waits until it is twice as long.

practice: Trace it on a map, real or in your mind: start in Kufa, go west to Istanbul and up to Sarajevo, east across the Caspian to Bukhara and Samarkand, then south through Afghanistan to Lahore, Delhi and Dhaka.
In each city, picture one person standing for the afternoon prayer, a little later than their neighbor. If you pray, you can remember the Muslims of one of those cities by name.

wordCard.voice: Where it's followed. The Hanafi school runs through Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia, carried by its judges and by empires that made it the law of their courts. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a way that someone goes; in law, a school such as the Hanafi school.

carryVoice: Your line: the most followed school. From Kufa to Dhaka, carried by courts and judges. Until tomorrow.
